messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always taken pride in his work as an interior designer, transforming spaces to evoke emotions and tell stories. But since his captivity during a business trip to Egypt seven years ago, every aspect of his life has become a carefully choreographed dance around fear. The memory of the event still bursts into his mind suddenly, like a door slamming shut - the sound of Arabic shouting, the feeling of helplessness as he was held against his will. These intrusive memories set off a chain reaction, making him rehearse conversations before any interaction, just to feel prepared for the worst. He avoids enclosed spaces, opting instead for open areas where he can see the room and keep his back to a wall - a habit that has become second nature. Even going to work or studying feels like a daunting task, as if the act of being confined in an office or classroom will trigger another episode. The memories themselves are still fragmented and difficult to articulate. Sometimes Kai recalls what happened but feels completely numb, as if it happened to someone else. When he tries to explain, the words get jumbled and he can't finish the story. The auditory recall is the worst - the shouting in Arabic still echoes in his head, a constant reminder of his vulnerability. Kai's body reacts before his mind even has time to process the danger, leaving him with strong negative feelings like fear, horror, and shame. He feels unsafe unless he can see the room, his back against a wall - it's as if his entire nervous system is on high alert, constantly scanning for threats. This perpetual sense of threat colors every interaction, making him feel like he's walking on eggshells. As Kai navigates his daily life, these maladaptive strategies have become more ingrained, influencing even the way he approaches memories of the event. He avoids thinking about it altogether, not just because it's painful but also because he fears getting stuck in the same emotional quicksand. But when memories do resurface, they reinforce his sense of threat - the feelings of fear and helplessness flood back, making him wonder if he'll ever be able to break free. Despite his best efforts, Kai can't shake off the feeling that he's constantly on edge, waiting for the next trigger to set everything off again. His friends and family have grown concerned about his increasing reclusiveness, but Kai feels like he has no choice - it's either retreat from the world or risk being overwhelmed by the memories and emotions that still haunt him. It was only when Kai realized he couldn't design a new home for his niece's growing family without having a panic attack in the middle of the project that he finally acknowledged he needed help. He's hoping therapy will teach him how to quiet the shouting in his head, to relearn how to navigate spaces and conversations without feeling like he's walking through a minefield. As Kai takes this tentative first step towards healing, he can't help but wonder - what if I never find my way back?
